title: No Depression Wasn't One Sound: The Indie-Country Diaspora (1990–2001)
author: Claudette
description: From Uncle Tupelo’s punk-country collision to Drag City outsiders, Nashville’s strange orchestra, and the roots-music afterlife in slowcore and experimental rock.

essay:
Uncle Tupelo’s 1990 debut gave this playlist its name, but the point is not to declare one band the inventor of a tidy genre. Jay Farrar, Jeff Tweedy, and Mike Heidorn carried punk’s abrasion into country, folk, and old-time material; then they made an almost entirely acoustic record, March 16–20, 1992, produced by R.E.M.’s Peter Buck in the five days named by its title. After the group split in 1994, Farrar formed Son Volt with Heidorn while Tweedy carried the remaining members into Wilco. Trace and A.M. are the two different answers to that fork.

The playlist follows that history into a wider indie neighborhood, not a row of direct descendants. Drag City’s Palace Brothers records put Will Oldham’s exposed, deliberately unvarnished songs beside the rough roots-rock current; Silver Jews’ Drag City debut Starlite Walker was recorded at Memphis’s Easley Recording and brought a Southern, road-haunted atmosphere into literary indie rock. Wilco, Son Volt, Vic Chesnutt, Smog, and Nashville’s Lambchop show how varied the decade’s roots music could be—from a road band’s country-rock to Callahan’s spare bedroom songs and Lambchop’s patient, orchestrated strangeness.

The coda moves into the next decade: Jason Molina’s Songs: Ohia brings the story-song tradition into slow, inward-burning form, while Califone’s Roomsound—an album Tim Rutili recalled began as a Red Red Meat project—lets folk and country instrumentation fray into studio texture. The shared thread is not a single sound or direct family tree, but an independent-music ethic: take voice, story, twang, drone, and room tone seriously, then leave the seams visible.
